claim: Each rod bipolar cell releases glutamate from approximately 50 ribbon synapses.
source: Each rod bipolar cell releases glutamate from ∼50 ribbon synapses (Sterling and Lampson, 1986; Tsukamoto et al., 2001; Tsukamoto and Omi, 2013; Mehta et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies and referenced in Figure 1A showing EM reconstruction with 46 ribbons.

claim: RBC ribbon synapses often exist as dyads with one AII and one A17 amacrine cell as postsynaptic targets.
source: These specialized synapses often exist as dyads, in which each presynaptic ribbon is shared by two postsynaptic targets, most commonly one AII (Figure 1A, purple) and one A17 (Figure 1A, green) amacrine cell.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the dyadic arrangement.

claim: AII amacrine cells have a compact dendritic field of approximately 40 μm.
source: They have a compact dendritic field (∼40 μm) and receive direct synaptic input from ∼10 RBCs.
evidence: Direct statement about AII morphology.

claim: AII amacrine cells receive direct synaptic input from approximately 10 RBCs.
source: They have a compact dendritic field (∼40 μm) and receive direct synaptic input from ∼10 RBCs.
evidence: Direct statement about AII connectivity.

claim: A17 amacrine cells have a wide dendritic field of approximately 300 μm.
source: They have a wide dendritic field (∼300 μm) and collect input from more than 100 RBCs, which provide their only known source of excitation.
evidence: Direct statement about A17 morphology.

claim: A17 amacrine cells collect input from more than 100 RBCs.
source: They have a wide dendritic field (∼300 μm) and collect input from more than 100 RBCs, which provide their only known source of excitation.
evidence: Direct statement about A17 connectivity.

claim: RBCs provide the only known source of excitation to A17 amacrine cells.
source: They have a wide dendritic field (∼300 μm) and collect input from more than 100 RBCs, which provide their only known source of excitation.
evidence: Direct statement about A17 excitatory input sources.

claim: Each RBC can make tens of synaptic contacts onto a single AII amacrine cell.
source: Central to our work here, each RBC can make tens of synaptic contacts onto a single AII amacrine cell (Tsukamoto and Omi, 2013), but typically only one synaptic contact onto a single A17 (Ellias and Stevens, 1980; Nelson and Kolb, 1985; Zhang et al., 2002; Grimes et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsukamoto and Omi, 2013.

claim: Each RBC typically makes only one synaptic contact onto a single A17 amacrine cell.
source: Central to our work here, each RBC can make tens of synaptic contacts onto a single AII amacrine cell (Tsukamoto and Omi, 2013), but typically only one synaptic contact onto a single A17 (Ellias and Stevens, 1980; Nelson and Kolb, 1985; Zhang et al., 2002; Grimes et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Spontaneous excitatory synaptic input variance in AII amacrine cells is more than 10 times larger than in A17 amacrine cells under dark-adapted conditions.
source: On average, noise recorded from AII amacrine cells (WT) was >10 times larger than noise recorded from A17 amacrine cells (unpaired t test p = 3 × 10−6).
evidence: Statistical comparison presented in Figure 1E with p-value.

claim: Spontaneous current fluctuations in AII amacrines had a variance of 1000 ± 154 pA² in darkness.
source: however, spontaneous current fluctuations observed in AII amacrines were much larger in amplitude (σ2 = 1000 ± 154 pA2, n = 20) than those observed in A17 amacrines (σ2 = 72 ± 22 pA2, n = 17; Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct measurement reported with sample size.

claim: Spontaneous current fluctuations in A17 amacrines had a variance of 72 ± 22 pA² in darkness.
source: however, spontaneous current fluctuations observed in AII amacrines were much larger in amplitude (σ2 = 1000 ± 154 pA2, n = 20) than those observed in A17 amacrines (σ2 = 72 ± 22 pA2, n = 17; Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct measurement reported with sample size.

claim: Deletion of connexin-36 disrupts gap junctional input to AII amacrine cells.
source: Deletion of connexin-36 disrupts the gap junctional input (Gjd2 knockout mouse, note: this mouse is also commonly referred to as the Cx36 knockout mouse; Deans et al., 2001, 2002); under these conditions, AII input currents continued to exhibit large variability in darkness (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deans et al., 2001, 2002.

claim: AII input currents exhibit large variability in darkness even when gap junctions are disrupted.
source: Deletion of connexin-36 disrupts the gap junctional input (Gjd2 knockout mouse, note: this mouse is also commonly referred to as the Cx36 knockout mouse; Deans et al., 2001, 2002); under these conditions, AII input currents continued to exhibit large variability in darkness (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Experimental observation in Gjd2 knockout mice shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Variability in AII inputs is insensitive to pharmacological block of feedforward and feedback inhibition receptors.
source: Variability in the AII inputs was insensitive to pharmacological block of the receptors mediating feedforward (to the AII) and feedback (to the RBC axon terminal) inhibition (Figure 1E).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1E with inhibitory cocktail.

claim: Large spontaneous fluctuations in AII inputs arise from excitatory RBC inputs and do not require synaptic inhibition.
source: Together, these results indicate that the large spontaneous fluctuations in the AII inputs arise from excitatory RBC inputs and do not require synaptic inhibition.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from gap junction knockout and inhibition block experiments.

claim: The largest spontaneous current fluctuations in AII amacrine cells are many times larger in amplitude and total charge than the average miniature excitatory postsynaptic current.
source: In support of this synchronization hypothesis, closer examination of the noisy AII input currents in Gjd2 knockout mice revealed that the largest spontaneous current fluctuations were many times larger in amplitude and total charge than the average miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC; see 'Materials and methods'; Figure 1D).
evidence: Observation from analysis of AII recordings shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Each A17 amacrine cell is contacted by approximately 50% of the RBCs within its dendritic field in rabbit.
source: Each A17 amacrine cell is contacted by a large fraction of the RBCs within its dendritic field (∼50% in rabbit, Zhang et al., 2002); therefore, pairs of A17s with highly overlapping dendrites receive synaptic contact from many of the same RBCs (i.e., RBCs that are common to both A17s; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2002.

claim: Pairs of A17 amacrine cells with highly overlapping dendrites receive synaptic contact from many of the same RBCs.
source: Each A17 amacrine cell is contacted by a large fraction of the RBCs within its dendritic field (∼50% in rabbit, Zhang et al., 2002); therefore, pairs of A17s with highly overlapping dendrites receive synaptic contact from many of the same RBCs (i.e., RBCs that are common to both A17s; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Logical inference from connectivity pattern, illustrated in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The peak of the cross-correlation function for paired A17 recordings in darkness was 0.51 ± 0.03.
source: Paired recordings from neighboring A17 amacrine cells (distance between somas < 80 μm) revealed strong correlations in excitatory synaptic input in the dark (The peak of the cross-correlation function in darkness, that is, the Dark CCpeak, was 0.51 ± 0.03, n = 8 pairs; Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Direct measurement from paired recordings shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Dim backgrounds reversibly reduced correlation strength in paired A17 recordings.
source: Eliminating excitatory synaptic transmission between RBCs and A17s with the AMPA-receptor antagonist NBQX eliminated the correlations (data not shown) and dim backgrounds reversibly reduced correlation strength (dim CCpeak = 0.34 ± 0.02, p = 0.0053, n = 8 pairs; Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Experimental observation with statistical significance shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: NBQX eliminated correlations in paired A17 recordings.
source: Eliminating excitatory synaptic transmission between RBCs and A17s with the AMPA-receptor antagonist NBQX eliminated the correlations (data not shown) and dim backgrounds reversibly reduced correlation strength (dim CCpeak = 0.34 ± 0.02, p = 0.0053, n = 8 pairs; Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Experimental result with AMPA receptor antagonist.

claim: The electrical resistance between highly overlapping A17 amacrine cells is 9.8 ± 1.3 GΩ.
source: Direct measurements of electrical coupling between highly overlapping A17s revealed an electrical resistance of 9.8 ± 1.3 GΩ (n = 6 pairs; Figure 3A,B), more than 30 times the average A17 input resistance (∼300 MΩ).
evidence: Direct measurement shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The electrical resistance between A17 pairs is more than 30 times the average A17 input resistance.
source: Direct measurements of electrical coupling between highly overlapping A17s revealed an electrical resistance of 9.8 ± 1.3 GΩ (n = 6 pairs; Figure 3A,B), more than 30 times the average A17 input resistance (∼300 MΩ).
evidence: Comparison of measured values.

claim: The average A17 input resistance is approximately 300 MΩ.
source: Direct measurements of electrical coupling between highly overlapping A17s revealed an electrical resistance of 9.8 ± 1.3 GΩ (n = 6 pairs; Figure 3A,B), more than 30 times the average A17 input resistance (∼300 MΩ).
evidence: Direct statement of measured value.

claim: Substantial dark correlations were present in A17 pairs with the highest electrical resistance (>15 GΩ).
source: Substantial dark correlations were present in pairs with the highest resistance (>15 GΩ), suggesting at most a small contribution from electrical coupling.
evidence: Observation from subset of recordings with high resistance.

claim: Spontaneous excitatory synaptic input to neighboring RBCs was at most weakly correlated in darkness (0.03 ± 0.02).
source: Spontaneous excitatory synaptic input to neighboring RBCs was at most weakly correlated in darkness (0.03 ± 0.02, n = 6; Figure 3E), indicating minimal correlations in the signals of neighboring RBCs due to rod divergence.
evidence: Direct measurement from paired RBC recordings shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There are minimal correlations in the signals of neighboring RBCs due to rod divergence.
source: Spontaneous excitatory synaptic input to neighboring RBCs was at most weakly correlated in darkness (0.03 ± 0.02, n = 6; Figure 3E), indicating minimal correlations in the signals of neighboring RBCs due to rod divergence.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from weak correlations in paired RBC recordings.

claim: Synchronized release from different synapses made by the same RBC dominates the measured correlations in inputs to nearby A17 amacrine cells.
source: Together these experiments indicate that synchronized release from different synapses made by the same RBC dominates the measured correlations in inputs to nearby A17 amacrine cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments ruling out gap junctions and upstream divergence.

claim: The measured peak cross-correlation of 0.51 ± 0.03 corresponds to a RBC CSS value of 0.80 ± 0.08 in darkness.
source: Applying Equation 1 to the A17 paired recordings, we estimate that the measured peak cross-correlation of 0.51 ± 0.03 corresponds to a RBC CSS value of 0.80 ± 0.08 in darkness.
evidence: Calculation based on anatomical measurements and Equation 1.

claim: Dim backgrounds reduced the synchrony of RBC output to a CSS of 0.52 ± 0.05.
source: Dim backgrounds reversibly reduced the synchrony of RBC output (CSS: 0.52 ± 0.05, n = 8 pairs; Figure 4G).
evidence: Calculated from paired A17 recordings under dim background shown in Figure 4G.

claim: In the dark, release from RBC ribbons is nearly perfectly synchronized.
source: This brings us to two key results. (1) In the dark, release from RBC ribbons is nearly perfectly synchronized.
evidence: Summary conclusion from CSS measurements showing 0.80 ± 0.08.

claim: RBC synaptic synchronization decreases with steady light.
source: (2) This synchronization decreases with steady light.
evidence: Summary conclusion from light adaptation experiments.

claim: APB substantially decreased both the holding current and noise in the inputs to AII and A17 amacrine cells.
source: APB increases mGluR6 activity and produces a clear reduction in the mean RBC synaptic input (Sampath and Rieke, 2004). APB substantially decreased both the holding current and noise observed in the inputs to AII and A17 amacrine cells, indicating that release from RBCs had been strongly suppressed (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: APB strongly suppresses release from RBCs.
source: APB substantially decreased both the holding current and noise observed in the inputs to AII and A17 amacrine cells, indicating that release from RBCs had been strongly suppressed (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Inference from the effect of APB on postsynaptic currents.

claim: A mixture of mGluR6 agonist and antagonist can suppress RBC voltage fluctuations while permitting control of mean RBC voltage.
source: A mixture of receptor agonist and antagonist should suppress RBC voltage fluctuations while permitting control of the mean RBC voltage and release rate via changes in the agonist/antagonist ratio (Ala-Laurila et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ala-Laurila et al., 2011 and experimental design.

claim: Antagonist concentrations could be identified that produced postsynaptic holding currents near those in darkness.
source: Indeed, antagonist concentrations could be identified that produced postsynaptic holding currents, and hence RBC synaptic release rates, near those in darkness (dashed lines in Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The agonist/antagonist mixture did not restore noise in the inputs to AII and A17 amacrine cells to its dark level.
source: This manipulation, however, did not restore noise in the inputs to AII and A17 amacrine cells to its dark level; the suppression of noise was particularly clear in the AII inputs (Figure 5C).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Similar release rates can produce very different levels of synaptic noise depending on RBC voltage fluctuations.
source: Thus similar release rates (dark vs appropriate agonist/antagonist mixture) can produce very different levels of synaptic noise.
evidence: Conclusion from comparing dark and APB+LY conditions.

claim: Suppressing RBC synaptic release with APB eliminated correlations in A17 pairs to 4 ± 2% of that in darkness.
source: Suppressing RBC synaptic release with APB eliminated correlations (4 ± 2% of that in darkness).
evidence: Experimental result from paired A17 recordings with APB.

claim: Restoring mean release rate with mGluR6 antagonist produced a peak correlation of 0.11 ± 0.03, corresponding to an estimated CSS of 0.18 ± 0.05.
source: Restoring the mean release rate with the mGluR6 antagonist modestly increased correlation strength (compared to APB), but it remained significantly less than that in the dark (peak correlation 0.11 ± 0.03, corresponding to an estimated CSS of 0.18 ± 0.05, p = 0.0034, Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Experimental measurement and calculation shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: CSS strength depends on whether noise in the RBC output is produced by upstream sources or is intrinsic to the synapse.
source: These results indicate that CSS strength depends on whether noise in the RBC output is produced by upstream sources or is intrinsic to the synapse (Figure 5).
evidence: Conclusion from pharmacological manipulation experiments.

claim: High CSS in the dark is generated by fluctuations in RBC dendritic input and the resulting fluctuations in RBC voltage.
source: Specifically, high CSS in the dark is generated by fluctuations in RBC dendritic input and the resulting fluctuations in RBC voltage.
evidence: Conclusion from experiments showing CSS depends on upstream voltage fluctuations.

claim: The variance of RBC signals changed by less than a factor of two across a 1000-fold range of light levels (∼0.5-500 R*/rod/s).
source: The variance of the RBC signals changed by less than a factor of two across this luminance range (Figure 6A,D), while the variance of the AII amacrine signals decreased 10-fold (Ke et al., 2014) (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 6A,D.

claim: The variance of AII amacrine signals decreased 10-fold across a 1000-fold range of light levels.
source: The variance of the RBC signals changed by less than a factor of two across this luminance range (Figure 6A,D), while the variance of the AII amacrine signals decreased 10-fold (Ke et al., 2014) (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 6B,D and supported by citation.

claim: AII noise decreased in retinas lacking gap junctions between AII dendrites and On cone bipolar axons.
source: AII noise also decreased in retinas lacking gap junctions between AII dendrites and On cone bipolar axons (i.e., Gjd2 knockout mouse; Figure 6D), indicating it was a property of the RBC input to the AII.
evidence: Experimental observation in Gjd2 knockout mice shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Noise recorded from RBCs remained relatively constant across 0.5 to 500 R*/rod/s in voltage clamp.
source: Noise recorded from RBCs remained relatively constant across this range of backgrounds (comparison of noise at 500 relative to 0.5 R*/rod/s, V-clamp: p = 0.92, n = 7; I-clamp: p = 0.18, n = 4)
evidence: Statistical comparison of RBC noise at different light levels.

claim: Noise recorded from AII amacrines was reduced approximately 10-fold from 0.5 to 500 R*/rod/s.
source: while noise recorded from AII amacrines was reduced ∼10-fold (comparison of noise at 500 relative to 0.5 R*/rod/s, V-clamp: p = 0.0039, n = 5; I-clamp: p = 0.019, n = 5).
evidence: Statistical comparison of AII noise at different light levels.

claim: Steady light changed the kinetics of the noise in the AII inputs more than the kinetics of noise in the RBC voltage.
source: Steady light changed the kinetics of the noise in the AII inputs more than the kinetics of noise in the RBC voltage, as determined from autocorrelograms (Figure 6E).
evidence: Comparison of autocorrelation functions shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The broad temporal correlations characteristic of AII input currents at 0.5 R*/rod/s were largely absent at 500 R*/rod/s.
source: Specifically, the broad temporal correlations characteristic of the AII input currents at 0.5 R*/rod/s or in the dark were largely absent at 500 R*/rod/s, while the kinetics of the voltage fluctuations in presynaptic RBCs changed relatively little (Figure 6E).
evidence: Observation from autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Steady light producing 500 R*/rod/s reduced the peak correlations in A17 pairs by more than approximately 50%.
source: Steady light producing 500 R*/rod/s reduced the peak correlations by more than ∼50% (Figure 6G) and reduced the estimated CSS to 0.36 ± 0.08 (Figure 6H).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Steady light producing 500 R*/rod/s reduced the estimated CSS to 0.36 ± 0.08.
source: Steady light producing 500 R*/rod/s reduced the peak correlations by more than ∼50% (Figure 6G) and reduced the estimated CSS to 0.36 ± 0.08 (Figure 6H).
evidence: Calculation from paired A17 recordings shown in Figure 6H.

claim: CSS of the RBC output synapses decreases with increasing light level.
source: The experiments in this section indicate that CSS of the RBC output synapses decreases with increasing light level, such that the synapses becomes less sensitive to fluctuations in RBC voltage.
evidence: Summary conclusion from light adaptation experiments.

claim: The increase in mean RBC voltage with increasing light level produces presynaptic depression by reducing the pool of available vesicles at the RBC→AII synapse.
source: This result is consistent with recent studies showing that the increase in mean RBC voltage with increasing light level produces presynaptic depression by reducing the pool of available vesicles at the RBC→AII synapse (Dunn and Rieke, 2008; Jarsky et al., 2011; Oesch and Diamond, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Excitatory inputs to On alpha RGCs at low light levels originate from modulation of On cone bipolar synaptic output via electrical coupling with AII amacrine cells.
source: At low light levels, excitatory inputs to On alpha RGCs originate from modulation of the On cone bipolar synaptic output via electrical coupling with AII amacrine cells, while inhibitory input to Off sustained RGCs originates directly from glycinergic output of the AII (Murphy and Rieke, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murphy and Rieke, 2008.

claim: Inhibitory input to Off sustained RGCs at low light levels originates directly from glycinergic output of the AII.
source: At low light levels, excitatory inputs to On alpha RGCs originate from modulation of the On cone bipolar synaptic output via electrical coupling with AII amacrine cells, while inhibitory input to Off sustained RGCs originates directly from glycinergic output of the AII (Murphy and Rieke, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murphy and Rieke, 2008.

claim: Excitatory input to On alpha RGC and inhibitory input to Off sustained RGC were highly correlated in the dark with a CCpeak of 0.43 ± 0.04.
source: Excitatory input to the On alpha RGC and inhibitory input to the Off sustained RGC were highly correlated in the dark (CCpeak = 0.43 ± 0.04, n = 5 pairs; Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Direct measurement from paired RGC recordings shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: Dim steady light (0.5 R*/rod/s) increased tonic synaptic input to On alpha and Off sustained RGCs but decreased correlations in synaptic inputs.
source: Dim steady light (0.5 R*/rod/s) increased tonic synaptic input to the two cells but, if anything, decreased correlations in synaptic inputs (CCpeak = 0.38 ± 0.04, n = 5 pairs; Figure 7C).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Bath application of APB eliminated correlated activity in On alpha-Off sustained RGC pairs.
source: Bath application of the mGluR6 agonist APB suppressed synaptic input and eliminated correlated activity in On alpha-Off sustained RGC pairs (Figure 7D).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Adding LY341495 to restore RBC release to near-dark levels produced weak correlations in synaptic input with CCpeak = 0.06 ± 0.05.
source: Adding the mGluR6 antagonist LY341495 to restore RBC release to near-dark levels (but with low CSS, see Figure 5) produced weak correlations in synaptic input (CCpeak = 0.06 ± 0.05, n = 4 pairs).
evidence: Experimental measurement from paired RGC recordings.

claim: High CSS at the RBC→AII synapse plays an important role in creating ganglion cell correlations in darkness.
source: Thus, correlations in the RGC synaptic inputs and CSS observed in the RBC synaptic output share a similar dependence on normal dendritic input to RBCs from rod photoreceptors, suggesting that high CSS at the RBC→AII synapse plays an important role in creating ganglion cell correlations in darkness.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from parallel effects of manipulations on CSS and RGC correlations.

claim: A combination of CSS and redundant connections between RBCs and AII amacrine cells help to amplify and transmit small modulations in RBC voltage.
source: A combination of CSS and redundant connections between RBCs and AII amacrine cells help to amplify and transmit small modulations in RBC voltage, whether noise or signals, and by doing so mitigate the impact of noise intrinsic to downstream synapses.
evidence: Summary conclusion from all experiments.

claim: Synchrony across different RBC output synapses was approximately 80% in the dark.
source: We found that synchrony across different RBC output synapses was very strong in the dark, such that ∼80% of the vesicle release events occurring at different ribbons within the same RBC axon terminal were synchronous.
evidence: Summary of CSS measurements in darkness.

claim: High level of cross-synaptic synchrony caused noise in the synaptic inputs to AII amacrine cells to be dominated by noise generated in the rod photoreceptors.
source: The high level of cross-synaptic synchrony caused noise in the synaptic inputs to AII amacrine cells to be dominated by noise generated in the rod photoreceptors rather than noise generated at the RBC output synapse itself.
evidence: Conclusion from CSS measurements and noise analysis.

claim: Vesicle release at the RBC→AII synapse transitioned from high CSS to low CSS as light level increased.
source: As light level increased, conditions under which other retinal circuits become active (Manookin et al., 2008), vesicle release at the RBC→AII synapse transitioned from high CSS to low CSS, thus limiting transmission of upstream signals and noise.
evidence: Summary of light adaptation effects on CSS.

claim: Behavioral sensitivity requires that rod photoreceptors detect single photons.
source: For example, behavioral sensitivity requires that rod photoreceptors detect single photons, and we now have a good understanding of how that is achieved mechanistically (reviewed by Rieke and Baylor, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Rieke and Baylor, 1998.

claim: Behavioral sensitivity requires that retinal synapses maintain low noise so as not to obscure the single photon responses of the rods.
source: Behavioral sensitivity also requires that retinal synapses maintain low noise so as not to obscure the single photon responses of the rods.
evidence: Logical requirement for single photon detection.

claim: In complete darkness, saturation of the postsynaptic metabotropic cascade suppresses the transmission of rod noise.
source: In complete darkness, saturation of the postsynaptic metabotropic cascade suppresses the transmission of rod noise; this synaptic saturation enhances the sensitivity of retinal signals more than 10-fold (van Rossum and Smith, 1998; Field and Rieke, 2002; Berntson et al., 2004; Sampath and Rieke, 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Synaptic saturation at the rod-RBC synapse enhances the sensitivity of retinal signals more than 10-fold.
source: In complete darkness, saturation of the postsynaptic metabotropic cascade suppresses the transmission of rod noise; this synaptic saturation enhances the sensitivity of retinal signals more than 10-fold (van Rossum and Smith, 1998; Field and Rieke, 2002; Berntson et al., 2004; Sampath and Rieke, 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Achieving the estimated dark CSS of 0.8 requires that dark fluctuations in RBC voltage produce near-deterministic changes in vesicle release at individual synapses.
source: Quite surprisingly, achieving the estimated dark CSS of 0.8 requires that the dark fluctuations in RBC voltage produce near-deterministic changes in vesicle release at individual synapses (Figure 8A).
evidence: Inference from CSS measurements and modeling shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Each RBC ribbon has approximately 10 active zones.
source: Multiple release sites at each ribbon synapse (each RBC ribbon has ∼10 active zones; Figure 8B), high vesicle availability and postsynaptic receptor saturation (Tong and Jahr, 1994) (Figure 8C) will facilitate low synaptic variability.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: High vesicle availability and postsynaptic receptor saturation facilitate low synaptic variability.
source: Multiple release sites at each ribbon synapse (each RBC ribbon has ∼10 active zones; Figure 8B), high vesicle availability and postsynaptic receptor saturation (Tong and Jahr, 1994) (Figure 8C) will facilitate low synaptic variability.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tong and Jahr, 1994 and illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: The low rate of ongoing release in darkness ensures that the readily releasable vesicle pool in the RBC terminal remains full.
source: The low rate of ongoing release in darkness compared to that in the presence of steady light ensures that the readily releasable vesicle pool in the RBC terminal remains full (Singer and Diamond, 2006), an important component of strong synaptic synchronization.
evidence: Supported by citation to Singer and Diamond, 2006.

claim: RBC output synapses operate far from a regime in which vesicle release follows Poisson statistics.
source: These results highlight that the RBC output synapses operate far from a regime in which vesicle release follows Poisson statistics, and this is important for their ability to reliably transmit the small signals forming the basis of night vision.
evidence: Conclusion from CSS measurements and analysis.

claim: Cross-synaptic synchrony is a key determinant of whether anatomical divergence will produce correlated signals in downstream neurons.
source: Cross-synaptic synchrony is a key determinant of whether anatomical divergence will produce correlated signals in downstream neurons.
evidence: General principle derived from the study.

claim: Changes in CSS can control the strength of noise correlations produced by divergence without morphological changes in circuit connections.
source: Changes in CSS, such as with mean light level as observed here, will then control the strength of noise correlations produced by divergence, without morphological changes in the circuit connections.
evidence: Conclusion from light-dependent changes in CSS.

claim: A CSS measurement of 0.8 in darkness indicates that the coefficient of variation at individual synapses must be ≤0.5.
source: Assuming a homogeneous release probability, a CSS measurement of 0.8 in darkness indicates that the coefficient of variation (CV) at individual synapses must be ≤0.5.
evidence: Calculation shown in Figure 8A based on CSS measurements.

claim: Recordings were performed within approximately 4 hours of retinal dissection.
source: Recordings from slice preparations were performed within ∼4 hr of retinal dissection, and we specifically targeted neurons that were ≥20 μm below the surface of the slice.
evidence: Methodological detail.

claim: Neurons were targeted at least 20 μm below the surface of the slice.
source: Recordings from slice preparations were performed within ∼4 hr of retinal dissection, and we specifically targeted neurons that were ≥20 μm below the surface of the slice.
evidence: Methodological detail.

claim: A17 dendrites traverse approximately 40 μm of the inner plexiform before reaching sublaminas 4 and 5.
source: A17 dendrites traverse ∼40 μm of the inner plexiform before reaching sublaminas 4 and 5 (where they make the majority of their synaptic contacts with RBCs); r0 accounts for the length of these initial descending dendrites.
evidence: Anatomical observation used in modeling.

claim: A17 amacrine cells make the majority of their synaptic contacts with RBCs in sublaminas 4 and 5.
source: A17 dendrites traverse ∼40 μm of the inner plexiform before reaching sublaminas 4 and 5 (where they make the majority of their synaptic contacts with RBCs)
evidence: Anatomical observation.

claim: The electrotonic length factor for A17 dendrites is 32.3 μm.
source: The electronic distance (γ = 32.3 μm) for the A17 dendrites was taken from previous work (Grimes et al., 2010).
evidence: Value taken from prior publication.

claim: Synaptic contact between RBCs and A17s was defined when fluorescent signals overlapped by >1 pixel at all angles of 3D rotation.
source: Synaptic contact was defined when the fluorescent signals overlapped by >1 pixel at all angles of the 3D rotation.
evidence: Methodological criterion for identifying synapses.

claim: Only one recording came from each dark-adapted retina preparation to ensure recordings consistently reflected a dark-adapted state.
source: To ensure that retinal recordings consistently reflected a dark-adapted state, only one recording (single cell or paired) came from each dark-adapted retina preparation (i.e., slice or whole-mount).
evidence: Methodological detail to control for adaptation state.
